title: docs(solver): close three gaps the API review found in the rank contract
description:
Follow-up to #12, from a second review pass on the published API surface. None of these caused a failure; all were things the contract left to inference.

## `rank` must be deterministic, and nothing said so

`docs/ALGORITHM.md:912-915` promises that *"neither the choice nor the package named first in an error can vary between runs on identical input."* That holds only if the provider returns the same `rank` for the same `(pkg, allowed)`. The contract never required it — and simultaneously said *"nothing requires it to be a count, an upper bound, or non-negative"*, which reads as licence to vary it. A provider deriving `rank` from anything ambient would silently void a documented guarantee.

The hole existed for `count` too, but the word "count" implies determinism where "hint" does not, so the split is exactly when this needed saying.

## The I/O prohibition forbade the only good option for some providers

*"It also must not cost I/O that answering `found` did not already require"* was a normative **must not**. For a provider whose index answers existence cheaply but can only *count* by enumerating, that left violating the prohibition or returning a constant — which the next paragraph calls "legal, cheap, and a bad idea". The contract forbade the intended implementation and disparaged the only alternative.

Now a **should**, naming the proxies worth reaching for: in-range count before filtering, range size, a bucketed estimate. All beat both an enumeration and a constant.

## `allowed` is always non-empty

Propagation cannot empty an accumulated term, for the reason `PartialSolution.Decide` documents — but that reasoning lives nowhere near `Candidates`, so an implementer had to guess whether the case needs handling.

## A `best` of ∅ gets its own error

"Outside the allowed set" is true of ∅ only lawyerly, and it points a provider author at a range problem they do not have. The real fault is a `found`/`best` disagreement: `found` said something is available and `best` names nothing. Now says that.

The non-empty path's message is unchanged, which is why the two existing tests that assert on it still pass — I tried changing it wholesale first and they caught it.

## Migration note cross-referenced to the `MakeDecision` tightening

0.2.0's recipe (`found: count > 0`, `rank: count`) is behaviour-identical for the *ordering*, which is what it was about — verified across all four branches of `preferCandidate`. But 0.2.0 also tightened `MakeDecision` to require `best` be *contained* in `allowed` rather than merely overlapping it. A provider that had been returning a non-singleton `best` overlapping the accumulated term compiled and ran at 0.1.0 and errors now.

That was listed under 0.2.0's `Fixed`, so it was not concealed — but the migration note did not point to it, so anyone who followed the recipe and then hit `"outside the allowed set"` had been told the upgrade preserved behaviour.

## Not addressed here

The reviewer also suggested a **struct return** (`Candidates(pkg, allowed) (Candidate[S], error)`) so the next hint is a non-breaking addition, and a named `type Rank int` to make "only ever compared" visible at the call site. That is a reasonable call while there is exactly one external implementation, but it is another breaking change and a separate decision — flagging rather than filing.

## Verification

`gofmt` clean; `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` green across all four packages. Only behaviour change is the new empty-`best` error message.

title: feat(solver)!: split Candidates' count into found and rank
description:
⚠️ **Breaking change to a published API surface.** Stacked on #11 — review that first; this PR's base retargets to `main` automatically when #11 merges.

## The problem

`Provider.Candidates` returned a single `count` carrying two unrelated obligations:

| | consumed at | correctness-bearing? |
|---|---|---|
| whether it is **zero** | `decide.go` unavailability branch → `KindNoVersions` | **yes** |
| how **large** a nonzero count is | the version-choice heuristic | **no** |

Sharing one return value made the cheap obligation look like it required the exactness the expensive one wanted. "Zero exactly when nothing is usable" is an **existence** question — settled by finding one usable version and stopping — but a provider reading the old signature reasonably concluded it had to establish usability for *every* version in range. That is per-version work in service of an ordering preference.

## The change

```go
Candidates(pkg P, allowed S) (best S, found bool, rank int, err error)
```

- **`found`** is the correctness-bearing existence answer, documented as something an implementation must *not* enumerate to compute.
- **`rank`** is an explicit hint: any upper bound is legal, it is only ever compared, and it must not cost I/O that answering `found` did not already require.

Measured on a 932,861-package production index, a provider rewritten against this read **31.6× fewer** metadata records while producing identical pins and identical failure explanations across 200 real packages. That consumer lands separately.

## ⚠️ The ordering that had to become explicit

**An unavailable package must be worked on before every available one.** That used to fall out of zero being the numeric minimum. Losing it would *not* produce a wrong answer — the solve would still reach the same conclusion, just after deciding the available packages, fetching their dependencies and adding their incompatibilities first. More work, a different trace, a different package named first in an error, nothing failing loudly. Which is exactly why it needed pinning rather than trusting.

`preferCandidate` now states it, and `TestMakeDecisionPrefersUnavailabilityOverEveryAvailablePackage` fails without it.

That test can only fail because the `universe` fixture reports `math.MaxInt` as the rank of an unavailable package rather than `0`. The contract says `rank` is ignored when `found` is false, so that is legal — and deliberate: with `0` there, unavailability would keep winning on numeric minimum alone, and a solver that dropped the `found` comparison would still pass while the test asserted nothing.

## Verification

- **Mutation-checked.** Deleting the `found` branch from `preferCandidate` fails `TestMakeDecisionPrefersUnavailabilityOverEveryAvailablePackage` — and *only* that test, across all four packages. Restored and re-verified green.
- `TestMakeDecisionRankMayBeApproximate` solves the same scenario with exact and with constant ranks and requires identical pins, since a constant rank is the degenerate legal case of the hint.
- `gofmt` clean; `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test ./...` all clean.

## Migration

Mechanical: return `found: count > 0` and `rank: count` for behaviour identical to before, then make `found` short-circuit and `rank` cheap when convenient. Breaking changes ship in a **minor** bump per `CHANGELOG.md`'s stated policy while the major version is 0.

title: docs(solver): say what the candidate count is actually for
description:
`Provider.Candidates`' doc claimed **"The count drives §8's heuristic and nothing else"**. That is false: it also drives the unavailability branch in `MakeDecision` (`solver/decide.go:133`), which derives a `KindNoVersions` incompatibility and forbids the whole `allowed` range. The next sentence stated the real obligation, so a careful reader recovered — but "and nothing else" is the sentence a downstream implementer quotes, and one did.

## What changed

Separate the two obligations the single `int` carries, because conflating them is expensive:

- **whether the count is ZERO** is correctness-bearing, and is an *existence* question — dischargeable by finding one usable version and stopping;
- **how LARGE a nonzero count is** only feeds the version-choice heuristic, which this doc and both prose sources already call tunable.

An implementation reading the old doc as requiring an exact count is paying for the heuristic, not for correctness. That is the difference between work that scales with the closure and work that scales with the number of published versions.

Two corrections about `best`:

- It said `best` "must be a single version", and nothing checks it. `versionset.Set` exposes no singleton predicate (`Intersect`, `Union`, `Complement`, `IsEmpty`, `Equal`), so a range returned here is recorded as the chosen version and carried into `Solution.Selected`. Now stated as an uncatchable provider bug rather than implying a guard exists.
- The reciprocal claim — that `best` must lie within `allowed` — **is** enforced and tested (`TestMakeDecisionRejectsAVersionOutsideTheAllowedSet`), and is left as it was.

Finally, document that **an unavailable package wins the heuristic comparison for free** because zero is the numeric minimum. `MakeDecision` relies on that to reach its unavailability case promptly; it was undocumented; and it is precisely what anything that stops expressing unavailability as the smallest count would have to re-establish explicitly.

## Verification

Documentation only — no behaviour change. `gofmt` clean, `go build ./...` clean, `go test ./...` passes all four packages.

#18657 (Phase 4.3) is the `go-pyresolver` Python adapter, and it cannot consume this module

title: feat(report): explain unsatisfiable constraints from the derivation graph
description:
## What

Implements `report/` — [`docs/ALGORITHM.md`](../blob/main/docs/ALGORITHM.md) §9 — so a failed
solve can be explained instead of merely reported. Closes out Phase 4.2d of
rstudio/package-manager#18656.

`Explain` walks the derivation graph carried by `solver.Unsolvable.RootCause`: leaves become
statements of fact about packages, derived nodes become conclusions drawn from them, and a
conclusion needed in two places is stated once and cited by number.

```
Because no version of echo matches <1 and echo 1 depends on charlie 5, echo <2 requires charlie 5. (1)
And because charlie 2 depends on echo 1, charlie 2 cannot be used.
And because no version of charlie matches >=4, charlie 2 ∪ >=4 cannot be used. (2)

Because delta 1 depends on echo <2 and echo <2 requires charlie 5 (1), delta 1 requires charlie 5.
And because charlie 3 depends on delta 1, charlie 3 cannot be used.
And because charlie 2 ∪ >=4 cannot be used (2), charlie >=2 cannot be used.
So, because root 1 depends on charlie >=2, the requirements of root cannot be satisfied.
```

Design decisions worth reviewing:

- **`Report[P,S]`/`Line[P,S]` are generic**, and each `Line` carries the incompatibility it
  states plus `Cites []int`. So a consumer building JSON, HTML or a linked UI reads the
  structure instead of regexing prose, and still reuses §9's ordering and numbering rules.
  `String()` is the plain-text view. `FromError` covers the `errors.As` dance, and there are
  two runnable examples.
- **`Formatter` supplies the vocabulary this module is not allowed to have** — how an
  ecosystem names a package and spells a version range. It defaults to `fmt.Stringer`.
  "Every version of X" is detected through the versionset algebra (empty complement), never by
  recognizing an ecosystem's spelling of `*`.
- **No `Unsolvable.Explain()` method.** `report` imports `solver` and never the reverse; a
  method there would invert that the moment `solver` wanted it.

## Review round (second commit)

Two reviewer seats ran before merge — one briefed against §9, one deliberately unbriefed —
both with **no web tools**, so neither could reach a reference implementation. RoboRev also
passed with no issues. The unbriefed seat found the most important defect in the change.
Fixed in `b770ddf`:

1. **An unconstrained dependency read as its own opposite.** A dependency is a *negative* term
   on what it needs, so an unbounded range there means "any version will do" — but every
   unbounded range was collapsed to "every version of X". `Requires-Dist: foo` rendered as
   "alpha 1 depends on every version of bravo", claiming all of them are needed at once. This
   is the commonest dependency form in both target ecosystems, and no fixture contained an
   unbounded range, so the branch was dead in the tests.
2. **An external root cause skipped the terminal wording**, reporting "no version of root
   matches 1" — blaming the user's own project for an unsatisfiable request.
3. A stale `numbers` lookup that could render one derivation twice; both causes being the same
   node (which `countCitations` guarded and `explain` did not); `assignNumber`'s zero return
   reaching the prose as a citation of `(0)`; and clause order left to map iteration when a
   `Formatter` maps two packages to one name.

**Every golden was unchanged by these fixes**, which is the finding rather than a footnote:
the suite agreed with the code, and the code was wrong. So the tests changed too — fixture
packages are words rather than letters (the fact-coverage check had been matching `"a"` inside
`"matches"`), it now demands the exact dependency clause so an inverted direction fails, and
phrasing branches unreachable through a solve are covered by a table over hand-built external
facts plus a caller-seeded unavailable fact. All five fixes were mutation-tested to confirm
their tests fail without them.

I also corrected two of my own documentation claims that were not supportable: the rarity
figure for the line-numbering shape (**the measurement is 19 hits in 500,000 generated
universes**; the "1 in 700" in the first version of this description was wrong), and a
determinism claim citing a run count the committed test does not perform.

## Independence

> Verdict: **PASS** · lineage: 3 sessions · log covers: 2025-03-20 onward

```
  paths audited     %gpb-worktrees/18656-report%
  authoring         1 session(s)
  lineage           3 session(s) including subagents

PASS: no retrieval of a known reference implementation in 3 session(s).
```

One authoring session — the one that wrote this change — and three in the lineage, because the
audit descends over subagents and picked up the two review seats. No unrecognized session is
present. The lineage growing from 1 to 3 after the review round is the audit working as
intended: it corroborates that the reviewers retrieved nothing, rather than taking the absence
of web tools on trust. Written from `docs/ALGORITHM.md` §9 only. No other implementation was read, and
both review seats were given agent types with no web tools at all, so retrieval was not
merely discouraged but impossible.

A second sweep of that session's own scratchpad (session-scoped, never the global pattern that
inflated the `#18655` lineage) returns `NO COVERAGE`, because no Go file was drafted there —
`find` reports 0 `.go` files, and all code was written directly in the worktree the first
sweep covers. Reported for completeness, not as a second verdict: exit 3 is not a pass.

Per the skill's own framing: a PASS is a statement about process — what was opened, fetched and
searched — not about what model weights encode.

## Testing

```
gofmt -l .                clean
go vet ./...              clean
go test -race ./...       ok (report, solver, term, versionset)
golangci-lint run ./...   0 issues, exit 0, v2.11.2 matching CI
```

Fixtures come from **real solves driven to failure**. `newDerived` is unexported, so nothing
outside `solver` can fabricate a derived incompatibility; rather than exporting a test-only
constructor, the tests take the constraint and only ever explain graphs the solver really
produced. That constraint applies only to *derived* nodes — `NewIncompatibility` is exported —
which is why the phrasing table can hand-build external facts directly, and why routing
everything through a solve was what hid defect 1.

Each fixture names the §9 shape it covers and `TestShapeOfEachFixture` asserts the shape is
still there, so an edit cannot quietly move a fixture and take the coverage with it. That
matters most for `reusedUniverse`, which covers §9's line-numbering case: a proof where one
*derived* incompatibility causes two others is hard to provoke — 19 of ~500,000 generated
universes, and none of the hand-written ones. Two findings from that search are recorded in
`CLAUDE.md` because they are easy to undo by accident:

- Its apparently irrelevant packages are **load-bearing**. They change which package decision
  making picks first, and hand-minimizing the universe destroys the shape.
- The solve is deterministic despite map-shaped inputs, which is what makes a golden over it
  safe.

Goldens are backed by invariants that survive rephrasing, since §9 is explicit that the English
is a matter of taste: every external fact is stated (as its exact clause, for dependencies),
every citation resolves to an *earlier* line, every assigned number is cited, `Cites` agrees
with the prose, and the render is deterministic — including under a deliberately non-injective
`Formatter`.

One deliberate deviation from §9, flagged for review: the "collapse an intermediate conclusion"
compression fires only when the derived cause is built from two external facts. §9 describes a
weaker condition for the one-derived case, which would collapse more aggressively; folding
three levels into one sentence reads worse than the extra line costs. Both reviewers noted the
divergence independently, so it is now documented at `collapsible` rather than implied. Easy to
tighten if you disagree.

title: Guard the two handling defects the deep review found
description:
## What

The first deep independence review (#6's `independence-deep-review`, run in a dedicated
session) returned **0 suspicious, 2 convergent, 3 forced** and recommended **no code change**.
Its actionable output was two *handling* defects. This addresses both in process.

### P1 — a review artifact reached a working tree

A similarity-review report was committed into a branch's `docs/` on 2026-08-04 and removed
before merge. It never reached reachable history — independently confirmed, the only match in
`git log --all --diff-filter=A` across those patterns is `CLEAN-ROOM.md`, the policy document
that later became `CONTRIBUTING.md`. But nothing *stopped* it.

Publishing such a report would create a discoverable record asserting resemblance to copyleft
code, which argues the opposite of what `NOTICE` defends. A new `no-review-artifacts` CI job
fails any tree containing one. It is mechanically checkable, which is the only kind of claim
CI is asked to make in this repository.

### P2 — context compaction is an uncontrolled channel

This is new information and the more important half.

Remediation happened in the session still holding the resemblance report, and **compaction
occurred mid-window**. Compaction *summarises*: review content can survive into the summary in
condensed form after the original messages are gone — invisibly, and with no way to inspect
what was kept.

That breaks the assumption the process was resting on, that detail scrolling out of context is
equivalent to it being gone. It is not. **A session that has seen a similarity finding is
contaminated until it is closed**, and closing it is the only reliable remedy. Recorded in the
deep-review skill — which now also says to keep reviews short, so they are less likely to
compact at all — and in `CLAUDE.md`.

## Testing

The guard is verified in both directions:

| case | expected | actual |
|---|---|---|
| review artifact staged | exit 1, names the file | exit 1, `FLAGGED: docs/contamination-review-2026-01-01.md` |
| clean tree | exit 0 | exit 0, `clean` |

Worth recording: my **first** attempt at that verification was itself a false negative.
`git ls-files -z` emits no trailing newline, so piping through `wc -l` reported `0` for a real
match and the guard looked broken when it was not. That is exactly the "a test that passes with
and without the change is not testing the change" trap `CONTRIBUTING.md` warns about, arriving
in the verification rather than the test.

Workflow YAML validated with `yaml.safe_load`.

## Independence

Touches no Go code. Provenance audit has nothing to sweep, which is the correct answer rather
than a gap.

Deep-review findings are deliberately **not** reproduced here beyond the counts, per the
skill's own rule.

title: feat(solver): conflict-driven backjumping, decision making, and the main loop
description:
## What

Implements the solver's remaining algorithm layer from `docs/ALGORITHM.md`: **§7 conflict
resolution and backjumping**, **§8 decision making**, and **§5 the main loop** that alternates
them. `report/` (§9) is untouched and stays for #18656.

Closes the work tracked as rstudio/package-manager#18655, and resolves all five design
decisions that rstudio/package-manager#19464 deferred to this phase.

### The algorithm layer, in one pass

**§7.2's satisfier arithmetic** becomes two per-incompatibility queries on `PartialSolution`.
The satisfier is the *maximum* over the per-term satisfiers — the incompatibility is not
satisfied until the last of its terms is — which the previous per-term `SatisfierOf` could not
express, and which §10 states directly ("the later of the two, chronologically, is D2"). A
caller that iterated terms and took the first answer got one chosen by Go map order, and on
§10's own state that answer is a *decision*, so §7.4's escape fires, the round of resolution
never runs, and the generalization the example exists to demonstrate is never derived. The
per-term primitive is renamed `FirstIndexSatisfying` so it can no longer be mistaken for
§7.2's.

`PreviousSatisfierOf` serves both of §7.2's branches with one query — the earliest prefix
that, with the satisfier injected, satisfies the whole incompatibility. Written as two
branches, each needs its own notion of "enough", and the case where both apply at once has to
take the later answer, which is exactly what a single search for the earliest sufficient prefix
computes.

**§7.3's resolution step** needed a constructor whose signature can carry two terms about one
package, because that is what unioning two incompatibilities produces and a map cannot
represent it. `NewIncompatibilityFrom` takes pairs and applies §3's per-package intersection.
In §10's trace that intersection is the entire content of the incompatibility derived. The
branch that used to sit unreachable inside `NewIncompatibility` is gone.

**§7.4's loop** truncates once, at a decision-level boundary, and `Resolve` returns the
replacement plus the package propagation resumes on. **§8** adds a `Provider` interface (the
solver still performs no I/O), the fewest-candidates heuristic, lazy dependency
materialization, the pre-commit conflict check, and the unavailability case. **§5** seeds the
root as a negative fact so the root is decided through the ordinary decision path and needs no
special case in the loop, in §7's floor, or in §8's eligibility.

### The five deferred decisions (rstudio/package-manager#19464)

1. **Decision-level numbering and the backtrack floor.** Numbering stays as it was, upholding
   §1's *main* sentence ("the number of decisions at or before that point"), which
   `TestLevelAlwaysEqualsDecisionCount` already pins. So the root decision is at level 1 and
   the floor must be **1** — not §11's resolved 0, which is correct only for §10's numbering.
   `baseLevel` reads the floor off the partial solution rather than hard-coding either, so the
   two cannot drift apart; it also fixes a case *both* constants get wrong, namely before any
   decision exists, where a hard-coded 1 escapes conflict resolution with a truncation that
   removes nothing and the main loop spins.
2. **`NewIncompatibility`'s signature.** As above. The inert-incompatibility fix from `d4b8ec2`
   is what makes the now-reachable `Positive(∅)` safe, and is untouched.
3. **`SatisfierOf` / `previousSatisfier`.** As above, including the rename.
4. **`Decide` and §8's eligibility.** `Decide` now **panics** on a version outside the
   accumulated term. This is a programming error whose effect is that every later relation test
   about that package answers `Satisfied`, so a real conflict cannot be told from state the
   caller has already corrupted, and nothing afterwards points back at the cause. `Eligible` is
   exported so callers can check first, and `MakeDecision` rejects a `Provider` that offers an
   ineligible version — so a misbehaving provider surfaces as an error from the solve, not a
   panic.
5. **§4's success criterion.** It is insufficient: an all-negative incompatibility of two or
   more terms is violated by a solution omitting both packages, while every relation test about
   it stays `Inconclusive` forever, so propagation never fires. Whether §7.3 can synthesize
   that shape from reachable inputs **could not be settled** (step 3 can contribute a negative
   term about the satisfier's own package, which alongside an inherited negative term would give
   two, but no reachable end-to-end trace was constructed). `Solve` therefore verifies the answer
   against the whole store in **completed-world** semantics before returning it — one pass, and a
   silently wrong answer becomes a loud error.

`docs/ALGORITHM.md` §11 records each resolution, per CONTRIBUTING's rule that disagreements go
there rather than being settled silently in code. §11 also gains a new item 8 for §4's gap.

## Independence

This library implements the PubGrub algorithm from its published prose descriptions. See
[`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md).

The checkbox this section used to carry is gone (#6). It asked the author to gate the author,
and an agent wanting a green build ticked it twice. A provenance audit replaced it — a
checkable fact about this change rather than a promise about it.

```
.claude/skills/independence-audit/audit.sh --paths '%gpb-worktrees/18655-backjumping%'
```

> **Verdict: `PASS`** (exit 0) · authoring: 1 session, 12 files, 2026-08-10 14:49–15:46 ·
> lineage: **15 sessions** including all subagents · log covers 2025-03-20 onward.
>
> No known reference implementation was retrieved anywhere in the lineage. Only two web calls
> were made in those 15 sessions, neither to a reference.

This corroborates the prose attestation below with evidence independent of the agent that wrote
it, which is the whole point — the previous wording asked you to take the author's word for the
author's conduct.

Scope, stated so it is not over-read: this is a finding about **process** — what was opened,
fetched and searched. It does not and cannot speak to what model weights encode. No checkbox
could either, which is why there is no longer one.

### The agent's attestation

`docs/ALGORITHM.md` was the working specification throughout, together with the existing
`term/`, `versionset/` and `solver/` code and the doc comments the Phase 4.2b review left
behind. No PubGrub implementation source was opened: not `pubgrub-rs/pubgrub`, not
`astral-sh/pubgrub`, not `uv`'s resolver, not any Go port. No web search was run. Where the
specification was silent or self-contradictory, the resolution is written into §11 rather than
inferred from elsewhere.

## Testing

`go build ./...`, `go vet ./...`, `go test -race ./...`, `gofmt -l .` (checked with **both**
the Go 1.25 toolchain CI uses and the local 1.26, since a doc-comment reformat between
toolchains would fail CI's format gate), `golangci-lint config verify` and
`golangci-lint run ./...` at the pinned v2.11.2 — all clean, lint run from the module root
because a path outside it reports a reassuring `0 issues.` having scanned nothing.

**§10's worked example now runs to completion.** `TestSection10Trace` was extended rather than
replaced, as CONTRIBUTING asks: it walks the satisfier arithmetic, the previous satisfier, the
round of folding in a prior cause, the exact derived `I4 = {http: [2.0.0,2.5.0)}`, and the
backjump. `TestSolveSection10` then runs the same universe end to end and asserts §10's final
answer (`app 1.0.0`, `http 1.0.0`) *and* that `I4` is in the store — a solver that reached the
right answer by retrying versions one at a time passes everything else and fails that.

**Both tests CLAUDE.md said were owed now exist.** `TestResolveBacktracksToTheRootDecision`
covers under- and over-backtracking at the very first decision, with a separate assertion for
each wrong floor; `TestResolveWithNoDecisionsKeepsResolving` covers the same floor before any
decision exists. `TestPriorCauseIsImpliedByItsParents` fuzzes pairs of incompatibilities and
checks the derived prior cause against every world over the packages involved, asserting that
any world violating it violates a parent — the property the whole algorithm's soundness rests
on.

**Every load-bearing test was verified by mutation**, per CONTRIBUTING: mutate only the
behaviour a test claims to pin, confirm it fails, restore. Twenty-four mutations across four
rounds, with a hard `go test -timeout` on each, because an under-backtracking floor makes the
main loop spin rather than fail. Four results were not simple kills, and each changed something:

- **A test passing for the wrong reason.** `TestMakeDecisionRejectsAVersionOutsideTheAllowedSet`
  offered version 99, which the test universe does not publish — so the error came from
  `Dependencies` rejecting an unknown version, not from the eligibility check. Deleting the
  check left the test green. It now offers a *published* version outside the allowed set, and
  asserts on the specific error.
- **A test asserting a law that does not exist.** A test claimed the order of §3's two
  normalizations was load-bearing. It is not: intersecting with `Negative(∅)` is the identity,
  and merging can only produce an always-true term from always-true inputs. Rewritten to pin
  the identity that is real, and the code comment claiming the hazard is corrected.
- **§7.3's step-3 condition is an optimization, not a correctness condition.** Firing it
  unconditionally left every test passing, including §10's trace. The term it skips is
  always-true and normalization drops it, so both compute the same incompatibility. Kept for
  readability, with `TestPriorCauseStep3GuardMatchesNormalization` pinning the equivalence, and
  recorded in §11.
- **`Store.Add` already deduplicates**, so §7.4's "add only if not the original input" cannot
  change what the store holds. Adding unconditionally buys something the conditional version
  lacks: whatever `Resolve` returns is *in* the store, hence findable by the propagation that
  must resume on it. The conditional version could hand back an incompatibility propagation
  cannot see, silently dropping the conflict — unreachable from `Solve`, which is what makes it
  worth closing rather than documenting.

Also tightened every `err != nil` assertion in the new tests to name the error it expects, since
any error satisfies the loose form — which is precisely how the first item above survived.

Refs rstudio/package-manager#18655, rstudio/package-manager#19464.

title: Stop the scratchpad pattern from inflating the audit lineage
description:
## What

Found by using #6's audit on its first real pull request, which is the only way this
would have surfaced.

#6 told you to always add a scratchpad pattern, on the reasoning that code gets drafted under
`/private/tmp/.../<session-id>/scratchpad/` and a sweep that misses it reports a clean lineage
that never existed. That reasoning is sound. The pattern was not: the scratchpad path is **not
branch-scoped**, so a global `%/scratchpad/gpb/%` matches every session that ever drafted this
library's code anywhere, and every match drags its entire session tree into the lineage.

Running it on the `#18655` branch:

| invocation | authoring | lineage | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--paths '%gpb-worktrees/18655-backjumping%'` | 1 | 15 | `PASS` |
| ...plus `--paths '%/scratchpad/gpb/%'` | 2 | **37** | **`REVIEW`** |

The second verdict is false. The extra session drafted go-pubgrub probes in its own scratchpad
nearly a week before that branch existed, and never touched it. Guidance now says to scope the
pattern to the session — `%/<session-id>/scratchpad/%` — which the worktree sweep identifies
for you.

## The actual fix is transparency

Correcting the documented pattern is necessary but not sufficient; the next over-broad pattern
would fail the same silent way. The audit now **always prints which sessions it treated as
authoring**, with the file count and time range each matched, and warns when there is more than
one:

```
Authoring sessions, and the files each matched:
  agent-a4cd8ec4c83d2fd20  12  2026-08-10T14:49:47.931Z  2026-08-10T15:46:16.977Z
```

A verdict whose scope you cannot see is not worth much. This would have made the bug obvious on
the first run rather than the second.

## Testing

All four exit paths re-verified, plus the new warning:

| control | expected | actual |
|---|---|---|
| `#18655`, corrected invocation | `PASS` / 0 | `PASS` / 0, **1** authoring session, 15 lineage |
| 2026-08-04/05 window | `REVIEW` / 2 | `REVIEW` / 2 |
| non-existent path | `NO COVERAGE` / 3 | `NO COVERAGE` / 3 |
| no arguments | usage / 4 | usage / 4 |
| over-broad scratchpad pattern | warns | warns |

`shellcheck` clean.

## Independence

Touches no Go code; the provenance audit has nothing to sweep, which is the correct answer
rather than a gap.

title: Replace the independence checkbox with a local provenance audit
description:
## What

Replaces the CI independence checkbox with two local skills: a zero-contamination
**provenance audit** run on every change, and an isolated **deep similarity review** run
before a tag.

The `confirmation` job greps the pull request body for a ticked checkbox. The body is written
by the author, so the check asked the author to gate the author — and an agent wanting a green
build ticked it, twice. A gate the gated party can open is not a gate, and leaving it in place
implied an assurance that did not exist. CI keeps the dependency check, which is the one part a
machine can actually know.

### The split

Two questions were tangled together, and only one of them contaminates.

**Process** — "did the sessions that authored this ever open a reference implementation?" This
is answerable from the project's own agent activity log, without opening anything forbidden.
`independence-audit` does it, and it is safe to run in any session.

**Output similarity** — "regardless of process, does the result resemble another
implementation?" This requires reading MPL-2.0 source, which is the act the claim says did not
happen. `independence-deep-review` does it in a dedicated throwaway session that never writes
this library.

### Design points that are not obvious

**Lineage is the whole session tree, not just descendants.** Climbing to the root first catches
the channel that matters most: a reviewer subagent reads a reference, reports to the parent, and
the parent relays it into a *sibling* subagent's authoring prompt. Descending only would miss
that entirely — and on this repository's history it is the difference between a 1-session and a
15-session lineage.

**`NO COVERAGE` is exit 3, not 0.** "No evidence of contamination" and "evidence of no
contamination" are different findings. The usual cause is a `--paths` pattern matching nothing,
which would otherwise report as clean.

**The permitted list is load-bearing.** `docs/ALGORITHM.md` is written *from* the Dart prose and
the guide's prose pages. An audit that flags them cries wolf on exactly the sources the policy
prescribes, and a detector that cries wolf gets ignored. `references.txt` subtracts them
explicitly.

**Findings are constrained in shape, because the report can carry the contamination.** A
reviewer writing "they do it this way, consider matching it" launders the reference's expression
into the implementer's context — then the report is the leak. So a finding is an anchor in *our*
file:line, a `forced`/`convergent`/`suspicious` classification, and divergence evidence. Nothing
else. "Cannot elaborate without contaminating, needs human review" is a complete finding.

**Remediation is briefed without the reason.** A prompt saying "this resembles X, rewrite it"
re-contaminates the implementer. The fresh session gets the task only: rewrite this file from
`ALGORITHM.md` §N, consult nothing else.

## Testing

Validated against three controls, all from this repository's own history:

| control | expected | actual |
|---|---|---|
| `#18655` backjumping work | `PASS` / 0 | `PASS` / 0, 15 sessions, 0 findings |
| 2026-08-04/05 review window | `REVIEW` / 2 | `REVIEW` / 2, 49 retrievals, 6 implementations |
| non-existent path | `NO COVERAGE` / 3 | `NO COVERAGE` / 3 |
| no arguments | usage / 4 | usage / 4 |

A detector with no negative control is worthless — one that always returned `REVIEW` would
"pass" the positive case while telling you nothing. Both directions are checked.

Also verified: the allowlist removes the permitted prose sources from findings (0 matches for
the Dart `doc/` pages and the guide, which the first draft flagged), and `shellcheck` is clean.

`.github/workflows/independence.yml` is not exercised by this branch beyond the dependency job,
which is unchanged in behaviour.

## Independence

No reference implementation was opened while writing this change; it touches no Go code.

> Verdict: `NO COVERAGE` · this branch contains no Go files, so the audit has nothing to sweep.

That is the correct answer rather than a gap: the audit's scope is Go authorship, and a
docs-and-tooling branch has none.

Refs rstudio/package-manager#18652.

title: docs(notice): repoint the dangling CLEAN-ROOM.md reference
description:
`NOTICE` pointed at `CLEAN-ROOM.md`, which was deleted in `232d832` when the audit records moved out of this public repo. A dangling reference in a licensing file is worse than most broken links: `NOTICE` is the document a redistributor reads to understand the independence claim, and it currently directs them to a file that does not exist.

Repointed at the two places the policy and its enforcement actually live now:

- `CONTRIBUTING.md` — "Implement from the published descriptions", the policy itself.
- `.github/workflows/independence.yml` — the control that enforces it.

Nothing else in `NOTICE` is changed. No code changes.

## One thing deliberately left alone, for a maintainer to decide

`NOTICE` also states that no other implementation's source "has been read while writing it". That sentence is a claim about the authoring process, and it is worth a maintainer's attention now that changes here are AI-authored: an agent can attest to the context it worked from — what it opened, fetched and searched — but not to what a model's weights encode. The sentence may still be the right thing to say, and the surrounding paragraph correctly frames independence as a legal property rather than a preference. But it is substantive legal text, so it is not being edited as part of a dangling-link fix.

Raising it here rather than changing it, and rather than leaving it unsaid.

title: feat(solver): incompatibility store + unit propagation; 6 correctness fixes and §10's trace
description:
## What

The middle third of the solver: incompatibilities, the partial solution, the incompatibility
store, and unit propagation. Conflict-driven backjumping and decision making are not here.

Implemented from `docs/ALGORITHM.md`, which is the specification derived from the published
prose descriptions.

| Package | Added |
|---|---|
| `solver/incompatibility.go` | `Incompatibility`, normalization, derivation causes |
| `solver/partialsolution.go` | Assignments, decision levels, satisfier search, backtracking |
| `solver/store.go` | Append-only incompatibility set with a per-package index |
| `solver/propagate.go` | `Classify` and `Propagate` |

## Independence

- [x] This change derives from `docs/ALGORITHM.md` and the prose sources it cites, not from
      another PubGrub implementation's source.

## Correctness fixes included

A review of this code against the specification produced eleven findings. Six are fixed here;
five are design decisions that belong with conflict resolution and are recorded on the issue
that will implement it.

**The one with real consequences: inert incompatibilities were firing.** `Positive(∅)` asks for
a version from an empty range, so it is false in every world. `Relation` returned `Inconclusive`
for it whenever the package was unassigned, following §2.5's *table* — whose stated
justification, "a version could still be decided later that lands in `r`", is exactly what
fails when `r` is empty. §2.5's own *definition* of contradiction gives `Contradicted`, and §2.4
says such an incompatibility "will never fire and never needs to be checked again". It fired:
propagation derived a vacuous `not ∅` for a package nothing had mentioned. `IsInert()` existed
and nothing consulted it.

**`versionset` violated its own canonicalization law** at the top of the universe.
`Exactly(maxInt64)` built a degenerate span and reported `IsEmpty() == false` while
`Contains(maxInt64) == false` — claiming to hold something while holding nothing. That breaks
`Equal`, and so makes the solver fail to recognize incompatibilities it has already derived.
Intervals here are half-open, so `maxInt64` is the universe's exclusive upper bound rather than
a member of it.

Also: `BacktrackTo` clamped the low side but not the high side, so `Level()` could exceed the
number of decisions permanently; `Kind` and `causes` could disagree in the direction that would
render a derived node *as an external fact* in §9's explanation walk; and empty
incompatibilities bypassed the store's dedup and index entirely.

## A self-contradiction in the specification, now recorded

§2.5's truth table says an unassigned package **satisfies** a negative term. §10's worked trace
contradicts that at steps 3, 4–5 and 6, and §6 collapses without the inconclusive reading — a
dependency incompatibility is `{depender: Positive, dependee: Negative}`, so satisfied-by-absence
makes every dependency classify as fully satisfied and nothing ever resolves.

The resolution: §2.5 describes a term's truth in a **completed world**; the partial solution asks
what the assignments so far **entail**. Different questions. An unassigned package is undecided,
not known-absent. Recorded as §11 item 8, which tells the reader to prefer §10 wherever the two
disagree.

Worth recording because this implementation followed §2.5 literally first and broke every
dependency derivation before being corrected.

## §10's worked example is now a test

Measured rather than asserted: with a mutation that deletes `SatisfierOf`'s package filter — a
plausible misreading of §7.2's "earliest assignment in the partial solution" — every
pre-existing test still passes and this test alone fails, on four assertions.

It deliberately does **not** assert absolute decision levels. §10 numbers the root decision 0 and
this implementation numbers it 1; which scheme wins is an open decision, and the backtrack floor
has to be chosen to match it. Asserting absolute levels would silently pick the winner. It
asserts the scheme-independent relations instead.

## Documentation

This PR also moves the clean-room process document and the two contamination review reports out
of this repository and into the private one, and replaces the attestation gate with a single
neutral confirmation. The reasoning is in the final commit message; the short version is that an
adverse internal audit should not be published, while forward-looking contributor guidance
should be. `CONTRIBUTING.md` is new and carries that guidance.

Note that the branch was **rebuilt rather than patched** — a commit that deletes a file leaves
the commit that added it fetchable, which is not a removal in a public repository.

## Testing

`go test -race ./...` green, `gofmt` clean, `golangci-lint` 0 issues, `actionlint` clean.
Coverage: `solver/` 94.7%, `term/` 100%, `versionset/` 98.9%.

Each of the four behavioural fixes has a regression test verified to fail individually with only
its own fix reverted. That mattered here: a mutation run found the suite already accepted the
broken and fixed forms of three of them equally, and one of my own earlier tests had asserted the
buggy behaviour it was supposed to catch.

title: feat(term,versionset): term algebra and version-set abstraction
description:
## Clean-room attestation

- [x] I attest that I have not read pubgrub-rs/pubgrub, astral-sh/pubgrub, contriboss/pubgrub-go, or any other PubGrub implementation source while writing these changes.

Written from [`docs/ALGORITHM.md`](../blob/main/docs/ALGORITHM.md) only — no external source was consulted while implementing, which is the point of having the spec. Swift Package Manager was not consulted.

## What

RFD 0001 Phase 4.2a. Tracked as rstudio/package-manager#18653.

**`versionset.Set[S]`** — the abstraction an ecosystem supplies: `Intersect`, `Union`, `Complement`, `IsEmpty`, `Equal`. Subset, disjointness and difference are **derived** from those rather than required of implementations, so an implementation cannot get subset and emptiness to disagree with each other.

The docs state the required laws and single out the one most easily violated and most damaging: **`Equal` must be true for any two representations denoting the same versions.** The solver compares terms and incompatibilities for equality, so an implementation keeping `[1,2) ∪ [2,3)` distinct from `[1,3)` would silently fail to recognize incompatibilities it had already derived, and could loop or report a conflict that doesn't exist.

**`versionset.Ints`** — a reference implementation over `int64` as sorted disjoint non-adjacent intervals. It makes the contract concrete and gives the tests a set that is obviously correct. It merges *touching* intervals, not just overlapping ones, which is what makes `Equal` reliable.

**`term.Term[S]`** — the algebra. `Negate` flips polarity and leaves the set alone. `Union` is derived via De Morgan rather than hand-written, and `Relation` is derived from the two degenerate terms rather than from case analysis over four polarity combinations — so it **cannot disagree with `Intersect`**. Hand-written case analysis over those combinations is where this algebra usually goes wrong, and the errors are silent.

I independently re-derived the three union identities from the intersection rules before implementing, since the spec derived rather than quoted them. All three check out.

## A design bug my own test caught

The polarity field is stored as `negative`, not `positive`.

With `positive bool`, the zero `Term` was `Negative(∅)` — the **always-true** term — so an uninitialized `Term` would silently satisfy everything asked of it. My doc comment claimed the opposite. Storing the inverse makes the zero value `Positive(∅)`, always-**false**, which surfaces as a conflict rather than as a constraint quietly vanishing. `Relation`'s zero value is `Inconclusive` for the same reason.

## Tests are exhaustive oracles, not tables

This is what #18653 asks for, and for an algebra it's the only thing worth having:

- **Set algebra** is checked against bitmask algebra over *every* subset of a 6-version universe — a complete proof on that universe.
- **Term algebra** is checked against a truth vector over every possible world for one package: absent, or exactly one version selected. That forces the **absence** world to be modelled explicitly, which is exactly where a negative term differs from a positive term over the complement set — the asymmetry the spec warns is easiest to get wrong. A dedicated test asserts they agree on every selected version and differ on absence, in both directions.
- Vacuity is pinned deliberately rather than discovered: an always-false term entails everything, so it reports `Satisfied`, and the oracle mirrors that precedence on purpose with a test naming the case.

## Mutation tested

Because 100% coverage on an algebra proves only that lines ran:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `Negate` complements the set (the classic error) | **6 tests fail** |
| Mixed-polarity difference operands swapped (the subtle error, yields plausible wrong answers) | **8 tests fail** |

Both reverted; tree confirmed free of residue.

## Verification

100% statement coverage on `term/`, 98.9% on `versionset/`; `-race -count=1` clean; `gofmt -l .` silent; `golangci-lint run ./...` at CI's pinned v2.11.2 → 0 issues from the module root.

## Not in this PR

The two ambiguities `docs/ALGORITHM.md` §11 flags — the backtrack floor and the joint-satisfaction correction — both live in conflict resolution (#18654, #18655), not here. They still need their dedicated tests when that lands.
